PAST, PRESENT, AND FUTURE
By Archibald Douglas, Lambda '94
<
^^m
Over a hundred years ago, at Union
College, on the banks of the historic
and lovely Mohawk in the then little
town of Schenectady, Psi Upsilon
was founded. The date was Novem
ber 24, 1833�an
epochal one in our
annals. It was
by no chance or whim
of fate that Union was the first home
of the four earhest fraternities. For
there. Kappa Alpha was founded in
1825; Sigma Phi and Delta Phi in
1827, and our own revered and loved
Psi Upsilon in 1833.
True it is that Phi Beta Kappa had
its
beginning at Wilham and Mary
in 1776, where it at first languished
and was later invigorated by Chap
ters at Yale in 1780, Harvard in 1781,
Dartmouth in 1787, and Union in
1827, but as Brother Jacobs wrote
in his Epitome of 1884:
Elections to it had come to be�as
they
now are�mere honorary rewards for under
graduate scholarship or of graduate emi
nence.
Phi Beta Kappa had, however, for
ever set the mark for the Greek let
ters and symbols that designate the
undergraduate fraternities or sorori
ties that now cluster about the cam
puses of almost every college in our
land.
Union, chartered in 1795, had be
come, in 1833, as it always has been,
one of our
outstanding colleges. Cer
tainly, in 1833, there was no center
of learning in the United States that
excelled Union in the loftiness of its
educational purposes and ideals. It
was then unquestionably the most
vibrant educational center in New
York State.
Dixon Ryan Fox, formerly Profes
sor of History at Columbia Univer
sity and, since 1934, the distinguished
and courteous President of Union
College, has taken a
deep interest in
Psi Upsilon and its beginning at
Union.
From his letter to us, we
quote in
part, as follows:
Most of the time from 1825 to 1830
Union was the largest in the United States.
Several times Yale got ahead of it, but
Harvard and Princeton were behind and
Columbia was much behind. There is no
question but that in 1833 Union was the
leader. This was not due so much to its
location or its fine buildings as to its fac
ulty and particularly to its President, Dr.
Ehphalet Nott. Dr. Nott was a remarkable
man� He had already become a Trustee
of Union, and in 1804, he became Presi
dent of the College� He remained as
President for sixty-two years, which I sup
pose is a record for aU Time�
745

ANNALS OF PSI UPSILON
You are of course interested in the situ
ation of the students in 1833. We had 232
in tlie College. Many of them had trans
ferred from other places. As you know,
the Dictionary of American Biography,
published a few years ago by Scribners
was an
attempt to bring together the biog
raphies of those who had really influenced
American life. I have been checking up
that work of the students who were in
College when the original Psi Upsilon men
started their enterprise. I find that among
those who were there from 1830 to 1835,
seventeen have been set forth at length in
the D. A. B. That is a remarkable record
for a
College of that size. I wonder what
lads in Columbia College or Union College
would be likely to be put in such a cate
gory fifty years hence. Among the men who
helped to found Psi Upsilon, or whom Psi
Upsilon men knew, were
John Bigelow, of
the class of 1835, the Journalist and
United States Minister to France; Henry
James, of the Class of 1830, father of
Henry James, the novelist, and Wilham
James, the psychologist; Henry S. RandaU,
the biographer of Jefferson�John S. Ray
mond, the first President of Vassar CollegeYou have noticed that the members of
the Delphian Society were in large part
the organizers of Psi Upsilon� There was
a double membership between the Society
and the fraternities. For example, Chester
A. Arthur, who was a Psi Upsilon and a
member of our Class of 1845, was also a
member of the Delphian Society.
New York State recognized Union's
e�Bciency by legislative grants from
the time of its start in 1795 to the
end of 1830, as
reported by the Board
of Regents, amounting to $332,135.46;
while, from 1754 to the same date,
Columbia in New York City had been
helped by the State Legislature in
the total of less than $93,000. These
old and probably unfamiliar statis
tics are
quoted only to prove what
many of us
may not realize, that
when Psi Upsilon was founded, her
foundations were
placed on solid
ground, near the campus of a col
lege that had already achieved much,
and whose fame was
rising rapidly;
whose worth was
recognized in a
tangible and satisfactory way in the
Legislature Halls of its State.
There, under the genius and lead
ership of its inspired teacher and
scholar, the Reverend Eliphalet Nott,
D.D., LL.D., whose fame stiU rings
down our
college corridors. Union
had become so
outstanding that she
drew unto herself students of back
ground, promise and serious thought
that, man for man, were not bettered
anywhere.
For those were the days when the
opportunity of winning a
college de
gree was
given, not as a matter of
course, but as a rare
privilege. It was
most often offered to the son or sons
selected for their scholastic profi
ciency, and the selection was
apt to
be the end of long, family-fireside
consideration and thought. Those
sons in the family whose bent was
toward pioneering, business or farm
ing, went other ways. This test was
begun in the Little Red Schoolhouse
(and it was red) and a
preliminary
aptitude and proficiency in the "three
R's" was
generally a
prerequisite to
"higher learning,"
Psi Upsilon, as thus founded, was
destined to draw together men of
kindred thought and sympathetic
minds, who passed on to successors
of their own selection the fine stand
ards of friendship, comradeship and
college loyalty set by President Nott
and by die builders of our "truly
laid" and well-founded fraternity.
Such a
group of proved and selected
students gathered at the birthplace
of Psi Upsilon in those pleasant years
of long ago. That the early brothers
of Psi Upsilon proved leaders, even
in the competition at Union that
President Fox writes of, there can be
no doubt.
746

PAST, PRESEN
Perhaps we
may be forgiven again
if we delve into statistics to prove
our statements. This time we
quote
from records of the first ten years of
the Theta Chapter, as set forth most
specifically in the "Twelfth General
Catalogue of the Psi Upsilon Frater
nity" issued in 1917.
We find that in those first ten
years, all of our initiates, excepting
two who died as
undergraduates,
were
graduated. One hundred and
six men were
graduated in those ten
years. Of these, forty-seven were
elected to Phi Beta Kappa; sixty-four
were "Commencement Orators" or
had some
prominence in the gradu
ating exercises; one made the Latin
Oration, and two delivered Latin
Salutatories�certainly an honorable
record in a center where, and at a
time when, excellence in scholarship
was a
prerequisite.
It may be interesting to note the
careers of these early Theta brothers.
Forty-four became lawyers; thirtythree, clergymen; nine, educators;
seven, physicians; eleven, merchants;
three, engineers; three, bankers; two.
Navy men; one, an author; one, a
joumahst; one, a clerk, and one is
described as a
capitaHst in after hfe.
Their accomplishments as recorded
in our Psi Upsilon Catalogue of 1917
were
astonishing. Hardly a man
failed to
distinguish himself in his
chosen walk�and, not seldom, na
tionally.
So it is pleasant to write so
easily
and
handsomely of our fraternal
forebears. But so far, we have writ
ten
only of their shrewd attainments.
That they were
good fellows, fine
brothers with cheer in their hearts
and a love for Psi Upsilon, we have
not
only the testimony of the seven
T, AND FUTURE
founders, but a
moving address made
by Honorable John U. Pettit, Theta
'39, at the Third Annual Reunion of
the Psi Upsilon Association of the
Northwest, at
Chicago, on
May 7,
1879, clinches our
proof.
Judge Pettit had received the hon
orary degree of LL.D. from Indiana
State University. He had been a
member of the Indiana and National
Legislatures, and was a
Judge of
the Indiana Circuit Court for the
Eighth Judicial District, so he is a
reliable witness, and worthy of quot
ing. In part, his speech runs as fol
lows:
I was not present at laying the deep and
solid foundations of Psi Upsilon. But I
know, very well and intimately, all its first
builders. From that early beginning, I have
seen the structure rise to its present perfect
proportions of strength, and grace, and
beauty. Looking out from my quiet place
in life, now, at the end of more than
forty years, never
forgetting all this time
the love and allegiance I bear it, and shar
ing the pride of every advancement; to
know, now, that this brotherhood counts
itself by thousands, enough to make an
army; rich in every scholarly purity and
culture, and all of high purposes; every
face turned to the front, at the restless call
of duty, and by achievement aheady won,
an
army with banners, we all may rightly
think this night, that the young associates
of that early time, almost "builded better
than they knew."
The Psi Upsilon was never a creed. It
was not set in hard and set form of words,
which were an exact measure. It was
something better. It was a faith�warm,
lively, living, buoyant, glowing, hopeful.
As understood by lawyeTS, our whole law
was unwritten law. Except in the mysteri
ous meaning of our name, and all it im
plies, between ourselves, and as duties and
rights, our manners, our manliness, our in
dividual sense of duty, and what should be
the paths, were all left plain and free. All
had been bom into a life of work. We
were
willing to prepare, and step forward,
and take up our
respective tasks. Life was
social�we became friends. Good work de
pends on who can do it best�we became
chosen friends. All honest life has common
747

ANNALS OF PSI UPSILON
duties�we worked together. The strong
are
stronger than the weak�we
helped
each other. With hke studies, tastes, piu:-
poses, ambitions, hopes, helping, and sup
porting and cheering each other on the
way, all grew warm and close to each
other, by very contact, and so close, it
seemed we could almost feel the beating
of every brother's heart. At its birth, and
in its cradle, Psi Upsilon was a marvelous
child of full health, and strength, and
beauty. In the old Theta, its brethren
were at the head of each class. They sat
in the highest seats of all the societies.
They more than shared all college honors.
From the beginning, the Psi Upsilon was a
free repubhc; but, better, it was a
family
of love.
May one, inclined to be old, dare to as
sert here an old man's privilege of
garrul
ity? In the lUiad, no one of all the neroes
mocked at the old, noisy, scolding Thersites. While thinking of this occasion, I
went to my little cupboard, that has an old
tin box in it. It holds early treasures. Here
is an old parchment, headed, "Chirographa Fratrum, P.U., in presenti, CapituH
Theta, datum Schenectadiae, die nono, Kal.
Aug: undequadrigesimo, octingentissimo,
millesimo, Domini Anno." This is supposed
to mean
JtJy, 1839. It was the parting
from college, with that painful word, that
has been and must be. It is the register of
our little community. It omits only two
names, Maunsel Van Rensselaer, long liv
ing by the classic shore of Geneva, with
Hannibal's path of conquest of the Alps in
sight, and Clem M. Davison, who presided
at the Detroit meeting last year.
We were a "merrie companie." Memory
warms. Now I recall it. The old attic,
perched at the top of three flights of stairs,
and just under the rafters, as if gone up to
roost, reached only with difficulty, like
climbing up the Mountain of Knowledge,
this was the first home of the Psi Upsilon.
Now climbing the ascent tried the acro
batic art! The long legs of Hesden King,
which a
good Providence had spun into
long-drawn gossamers, but whose head
was
always above the top of his class,
were, facetiously, supposed sometimes, to
reach down to the ground, through the
top cracks. But this statement is apocry
phal. If the high place of our habitation
meant anything, we
spent many Attic
nights. The place of meeting was
seques
tered in some odd comer of Schenectady,
not necessary to be told. We were hooded
monks, approaching our odd quarters by
twos and threes, and by devious and var
ious ways, lest oiu: virtues should be drawn
under suspicion.
Each one of these is now seen in his
own handwriting. The place and the per
sons now hve again in vision. Van Vorst,
so long an honored magistrate in the
chief seat of magistracy in New York, our
chief, with pleasing, honest face, and with
manners ahready magisterial; Monilaws,
with sparkling black eyes, always so much
in earnest; Lewis, our beautiful Apollo, so
good to look upon; Stebbins and King;
Van Ingen, with Holland phlegm, drawn
into himself, meditating future victories in
surgery. John M. Wheeler, who has so
long, and so honorably, husbanded the
riches of Michigan University, was our
dry joker. He fired them all with a slow
match-first, a little lifting of the ground,
then, the upheaval, and then, at leisure,
the vigorous explosion, that, like Yorick's,
"set the table in a roar." Roberts was the
only one gifted with the magic, but mel
ancholy, gift of poetry and song, which
neither larks, nor thrushes, nor
poets can
explain, but which plays with all our
heart-strings; and the fair, good face of
Dan Shepherd always glowed in a corus
cation. Thompson, and Stewart, and Schermerhom, and Dimning, and myself, were
the small boys, such as can be found in all
well-regulated famihes. Clarkson Nott Pot
ter, with so
many honors worthily won, at
the bar, and for so
many years in Congress,
was then the yoimgest of the family. This
was the old Psi Upsilon. AU present.
After finishing the regular work of the
night, there was no withdrawing of the
cloth, that hilarity might begin. Our pota
tions were water, pure and simple. The
diet of our board was leaner than the
feast of Apemantus. But it was, then,
abandon and rollicking; and fun, and jest,
and song, and love, and goodness, and
greatness, till the small hours of the morn
ing came, and we locked brotherly fingers,
with our chief in the midst, and with the
parting words, "All are One," went our
way.
Truly, those brothers of an earlier
day left us a fine heritage of good
fellowship. Yet Psi Upsilon's founders
-Goodale, Hadley, Martindale, Tuttie, Barnard, Harvey and Stewartare Psi Upsilon's glory.
748

PAST, PRESEN
Within our Pantheon of Fame
Deep let us carve each honored name!
Gooddale of righteousness and skill,
Hadley, whose precepts guide us still.
And that great leader tried and hale.
The wise, far-seeing Martindale;
Tuttle, the loved of all who knew
His sterling vision, soimd and true;
Barnard, whose early name recalls
The sacred ties of Theta's halls;
Harvey, whose benediction cheers
His Brothers of succeeding years.
And lastly Stewart, grave or
gay.
The solon of an earlier day;
Brothers whose warm
clasp handed on
The fine joys of Psi Upsilon!
For all our
generations through
They builded better than they knew.
They stir our hearts! Prophetic sight
Sees all our altar lamps alight;
And through the coming cycles long
We hear oiur harmonies of song;
Proud heritors of our
great past
We'll carry on while life shall last.
And guard with jealous care the bond
That ties our
past to years beyond.
The long romance of friendship
and brotherhood that began with the
primal clasp of the "Mystic Seven,"
handed down from handclasp to
handclasp, to those initiates at our
altars, decade after decade, and now
from century to century, has brought
and now
brings thousands upon
thousands of us
together in Spirit
through that sacred tie that holds us
together,
Psi U's foundations firm and good.
Support our ancient brotherhood;
Let our
gone fathers shape our way
In this mad world, and come what may
Their Sons will ever carry on
Their standards for Psi Upsilon!
Since the first Theta days, Psi Up
silon has "flourished like a
green bay
tree," Unlike the aloe, that is said to
blossom only once in a century, Psi
Upsilon flowered often, put forth
many branches, and bears much
fruit.
The essential purposes of our FraT, AND FUTURE
ternity have not changed in over a
century. Their basis is the bringing
together of companionable minds;
the friendship of men drawn close
by mutual ties and interests. In all,
the theory of selection applies. Com
radeship first brought the old Theta
group together. As youthful com
rades, they entered into pledges that
young men, selected by them or
their successors, with the same ideals
of fraternal friendship, in turn en
tered into. The "thoughts of youth"
in 1833 were
"long, long thoughts."
Soon after Theta was
firmly es
tablished, the process of expansion
brought men of other colleges into
Psi Upsilon. We will not repeat here
what has already been set forth in
detail in our
chapter histories. Each
succeeding chapter strengthened us.
We note our
century of progress
briefly. Following the Theta, Delta
was installed at New York Univer
sity on the Atlantic Seaboard and in
the New England and Eastern States,
other Chapters of Psi Upsilon were
founded at Yale, Brown, Amherst,
Dartmouth and Columbia, and our
far Eastern Chapter, the Kappa of
Bowdoin, began its long history in
1843.
In turn, Psi Upsilon placed Chap
ters at Hamilton, Wesleyan, Har
vard and Rochester, and in 1860 we
ventured as far west as Ohio; where
Iota of Kenyon signed our rolls. Aft
erward, with the Phi of Michigan
and the Omega of Chicago, we went
further westward; and in succession,
charters were
granted to Chapters
at Syracuse, Cornell, Trinity, Le
high, the Universities of Pennsylva
nia, Minnesota and Wisconsin, until,
in 1902, with the Epsilon of the Uni
versity of California, we first "looked

ANNALS OF
upon the Pacific." Then came the
Omicron at Illinois, the Delta Delta
of Williams and the Theta Theta of
Washington. Our last three charters
were
given to our Canadian brothers;
at the University of Toronto in 1920,
McGill University in 1928, and finally,
the Zeta Zeta at Vancouver in 1935
made our Psi Upsilon roll complete.
Some time ago, the writer was
privileged to be at historic Mulberry
Hall, on the Santee River, in South
Carolina. There, since 1741, its South
ern
hospitality has been graceful and
real. One of the glories of that in
comparable center of beauty and cul
ture, of sportsmanship and welcome,
is its live oak trees, clustered to
gether. There are
perhaps a half
dozen of them dating back almost
to the plantation's beginnings. The
writer walked under them rever
ently. The most beautiful in natural
contour, in all its circumference and
majesty, brought home a
picture of Psi
Upsilon. Its sturdy lower branches
reached so far that the drive passed
under them�they reached out from
the grand trunk, and, overcome
by
their own sturdiness, touched the
ground only to rise again with every
leaf and branch vigorous and per
fect. The Southern sun filtered down
from the tops to the lower spread
and played a
gossamer silhouette on
the ground. The writer stood beneath
this overtone of two centuries. It
seemed so like Psi Upsilon�every
branch in perfect symmetry, every
twig and leaf healthy and green, all
magnificent, and seemingly ageless.
From the fretted shade of that
great oak, he left with a
deep vener
ation, as if from a
Chapter Meeting
of Psi U. Brothers after the singing
of our
evening song.
SI UPSILON
The Psi Upsilon Epitome of Albert
Poole Jacobs, Phi "73, reprinted in
these Annals, gave an
embracing
summary of the achievements of Psi
U men
during the first half-century
of our
fraternity, from 1833 to 1884.
They were sturdy men, those broth
ers of fifty years ago�sturdier in a
way perhaps than the original seven.
For they seemed, at least at the Fif
tieth Anniversary Banquet, to have
become notable trenchermen and to
have continued their banquets from
early eve till break of day. It is in
teresting to take up the story from
the time of Jacobs' great Epitome
and give some reminiscences of that
notable feast, held under the auspices
of the Theta Chapter, as set forth by
Judge Dow Beekman, Theta '84, and
published in The Diamond of March,
1933, and to point out how some of
the Theta's financial problems were
met by the vision, courage and en
thusiasm of a
young Theta man, in
1883.
According to Judge Beekman, then
an
undergraduate, the expense of the
Fiftieth was more than the Theta
could carry, and written appeals hav
ing failed to bring enough "to pay
the postage on the letters" and local
solicitation still being unsatisfactory,
a
personal campaign was
planned in
New York City. Judge Beekman,
then a
Junior, announced that he
would go to New York and raise
"three or four hundred dollars."
I arrived, he writes, in New York on the
afternoon of the 21st of February, 1883,
went to the old Astor House in the lower
part of New York where Brother Ward
McLean, Theta, '43, real estate agent for
the Astor Corporation, had an office and he
had me
assigned to a room on the top floor
at a dollar a
day. At the lunch room, I
could obtain an excellent breakfast for
thirty-five cents and dinner at night for

PAST, PRESENT, AND FUTURE
sixty cents, including a
tip to the waiter.
In the morning, I started out to find
the Psi U's of the City of New York, and,
as I thought Wall Street had the most
money, that was
my destination.
He started at the famous banking
firm of Brown Brothers "as the B's
headed the hst in Wall Street," After
a time, he was received by Mr, Brown
in his private office,
"I told him where I came from and what
I wanted. As he probably had a
good
night's rest, he was not irritated by my con
versation and permitted me to make my
heartfelt appeal. Then I received another
good lesson in the ways of New York. He
said 'Young man, where are
your creden
tials? How do I know that you are en
titled to collect money for this purpose?
Here in New York, we are
besieged con
stantly for subscriptions and very often by
rank impostors.' I was stunned and began
to pull my diary and other papers out of
my pocket to prove my identity and of
fered to pay the expense of a
telegram to
the President of Union College inquiring
about my reliability and authority to repre
sent the Theta Chapter. Of course, I had
obtained permission of the President to be
absent from college and he knew what my
mission was. Mr. Brown smiled and kindly
rephed: 'No, no, my boy, you needn't do
that. No one would ever take you for a
sharper.
You have told me
enough,
and in a
way that interests me, and I will
subscribe twenty-five dollars in the name
of my brother and myself.'
He gave me the twenty-five dollars and
I gave him the grip and thanked him over
and over
again and I left him with a heart
full of courage and feeling hke a million
aire, and ruminating that my 'green coun
try ways and clothes saved me from ap
pearing in the 'sharper' class.' I want to
record the names of those brothers: Fred
erick A. Brown, Lambda, 'Y2, and Herbert
P. Brown, Lambda, '77.
I have forgotten some of the details, but
I think I later obtained a letter of intro
duction and recommendation from Brother
Ward McLean who was at that time Presi
dent of the Coimcil of the Fraternity and
soon after obtained the signature of Her
bert L. Bridgman, Gamma '66, and his
subscription for twenty-five dollars. His
signature was as
good as a letter of recom
mendation because he was well knovwi in
New York.
Francis S. Bangs, Lambda, '78, whose
father was a member of the famous law
firm of Bangs & Stetson, gave me twentyfive dollars, and his signature was an
opensesame in New York.
I remember my call on Burton N. Har
rison, Beta '59, who was the official private
secretary of President Jefferson Davis dur
ing the war. He was a
very stately man,
over six feet tall, of commanding appear
ance, exquisitely dressed. He received me
in the most beautifully furnished law office
I had ever seen
up to that time, motioned
me to a
large easy chair and said, 'My
clerk informs me that you say you are a
Psi U and a student of Union College.
What can I do for you?' I knew he was a
southerner, therefore, I believed he had a
warm heart and I opened up my flood of
language to tell him what a
grand celebra
tion we were
planning and that as Sche
nectady was too small, we were
planning
to have it in Albany which city he was
probably familiar with and would like to
visit. 'Albany!' said he. 'A place noted for
its corrupt politicians, stinking water and
the worst whiskey in the world! If you are
going to hold a real celebration for a
great
fraternity, you should come to New York.'
I explained to him that the Union Chap
ter was the Mother Chapter and that was
the reason why the celebration was in
charge of the Theta, but I diplomatically
took the cue he had given and boldly as
sured him that if we could raise money
enough, we
might be induced to hold the
celebration in New York, but I could not
promise it. He himself said, after he had
thought a moment, that it was
probably
best to hold it 'up state.' 1 then reminded
him that many boys from the South had
been students of Union College and that
Catharine Lorillard Wolfe of South Car
olina had endowed some scholarships at
Union to aid students from Southern states.
He knew about Dr. Nott and he asked me
many questions. I thought I was overstay
ing my welcome and was
wondering
whether he was
going to give me
any
money and arose to go when he said, 'Sit
down. It is a long time since I have talked
with a college boy and a Psi U who is so
full of enthusiasm for the Society as
you
are. It has brought back my college days,
and I am
going to give you twenty-five
dollars whether I attend the Anniversary
or not." By that time I had forgotten that
I was a
country boy and I had gotten
courage to carry out my mission and face
the biggest men in the City of New York
on the necessity of the success of the cel751

ANNALS OF PSI UPSILON
ebration of the Fiftieth Armiversary of
Psi Upsilon.
Frederic R. Coudert, Lambda '50, fa
mous international lavvyer and for many
years representative of the French Gov
ernment, received me like a
genuine Psi U
and kindly gave me
twenty-five dollars,
John Clinton Grey, Delta '65, afterwards
Judge of the Court of Appeals of New
York State, cheerfully subscribed twenty
dollars."
The fascinating tale of our first
half-century has often been told. He
who runs
may read, but the reading
has been made delightful by the deft
pens of many of our earher brothers,
now
gone, who have inscribed on
our scrolls the records of our
begin
